items.name: nanonets.ai
items.brief: 215 new stars and 17 new forks in a day, a fork ratio of 8.6%. Open issues went 37 to 62 over four days while stars rose 68%: adoption fast enough that the bug reports are keeping pace.
items.description: Graft, an open source context layer for coding agents, published by Nanonets as the repository NanoNets/Graft. It parses a codebase into a graph of symbols and the relationships between them, then hands an agent only the nodes a given prompt actually needs, rather than leaving it to grep its way around a large repository. It wires into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Gemini through an MCP server and editor hooks, and rebuilds the graph in the background after each turn, so the index never has to be rebuilt by hand.

items.name: xoreaxeaxeax/skitter-creek-bath-salts
items.brief: 491 new stars in a day, up 43.4%, and forks up 109 to 131, a fork ratio of 8.1%. Its first two issues were filed the same day, alongside 173 HackerNews comments.
items.description: A security research tool that attacks the memory hierarchy from underneath, by reprogramming the DRAM controller's address translation registers on AMD Family 16h processors, the last generation whose datasheets document those registers and confirm they cannot be locked. Remapping physical addresses breaks the assumption every platform security primitive rests on, exposing regions of DRAM the kernel itself cannot see: the Platform Security Processor, System Management Mode, C6 memory and CPU microcode.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: 13,544 weekly downloads, up 11.5% in a day and 200% since 4 August, while stars moved 0.5%. Seventh straight appearance, and the gap between installing it and bookmarking it has never once closed.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: TheRealYT/git-knife
items.brief: 291 stars, up 12.3%, with 165 HackerNews points and 101 comments. Open issues up 33.3% on the same day: the people who found it are using it hard enough to file bugs.
items.description: A desktop GUI for editing git commit metadata: the message, the author, and both the author and the committer dates. Existing git interfaces reword and reorder commits well but treat dates as fixed, and the tools that can rewrite them, git-filter-repo and commit-tree, have no interface at all. git-knife covers that gap by shelling out to the system git and rebuilding each commit from its original tree, so file contents are provably never altered.

items.name: antigma.ai
items.brief: Forks up 30.8% against stars up 12.7% in a day, 50 forks on 1,652 stars. Pushed the same day, and HackerNews has gone quiet at 1.8%, so the growth is running without a thread behind it.
items.description: Antigma, a terminal harness for running AI coding agents, published as the repository AntigmaLabs/ante. The agent loop, the tool calls and the sandbox ship in a single binary rather than being assembled from separate services, so the whole run happens on one machine and can be inspected afterwards. For a tool of this kind the fork count is the number that carries information: forking means taking the code away to change it, which is a different act from starring it.

items.name: AntigmaLabs/ante
items.brief: Stars up 14.1% and forks up 10.2% while HackerNews went the other way, front page presence gone entirely and posts down 33%. The thread ended and the growth did not. 34 forks on 1,443 stars is a 2.4% ratio, so most arrivals are still evaluating it.
items.description: Ante, a self contained harness for running AI coding agents in a terminal, published by Antigma Labs and also reachable at antigma.ai. It does the job of Claude Code or Codex without their dependencies or model constraints, shipping as a single prebuilt binary that is straightforward to drop into a container. The project is explicit that it is an alpha preview and that the core is not yet open source.

items.name: antirez/h3.c
items.brief: Stars up 117%, forks up 96%, open issues up 183% and HackerNews comments up 453% in a single day. 71 forks on 1,432 stars is a 5% ratio within hours, and 13 open issues means people are running it on their own machines rather than reading the README.
items.description: An inference engine written in C that runs the MiniMax H3 language model on Apple hardware, from Salvatore Sanfilippo, who wrote Redis. Its claim is that a model this size can be served from one self contained C program with no Python runtime and no framework at all. That matters because the usual stack is several gigabytes of dependencies before the model itself is even loaded.

items.name: palamim/starboard
items.brief: Second appearance, and stars, forks and open issues all moved together again at 3.1%, 3.6% and 20%. Pushed today rather than abandoned after the thread. At this size that is a handful of people, and it is the same handful coming back.
items.description: A macOS terminal that sits permanently beside the Dock instead of appearing on a hotkey. It stays on screen across every Space, including over full screen apps, and never takes focus from whatever you are working in. Inside it is a real login shell, so directory, history and state carry between commands rather than each one starting fresh. The bet is that a terminal you glance at gets used differently from one you summon.

items.name: MakazhanAlpamys/Soup
items.brief: 68 open issues against 430 stars is a 16% ratio, five times what a young repo usually carries, and forks are up 5.5% against 3% star growth. The people arriving are running it and hitting walls rather than bookmarking it. HackerNews has gone quiet at 0.7%.
items.description: Fine tunes a large language model from a single YAML file, with no SSH into a training box and no framework configuration to assemble. It streams layers rather than loading the whole model, which is what lets an 8 billion parameter model train on a laptop GPU with 4 GB of memory. Distributed on PyPI as soup-cli, so installs are countable separately from stars.

items.name: palamim/starboard

items.description: A news site covering the AI industry as it happens: funding rounds, model launches, infrastructure changes and founder moves, filed as short scoops rather than weekly summaries. It competes on speed of publication against the general technology press, so the interesting measurement for a site like this is whether readers arrive directly or only through aggregators.

items.name: xoreaxeaxeax/asm-hall-of-shame
items.brief: Stars up 38.4% in a day, forks up 12%, open issues up 20%, with GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters all seeing it at once. Lobsters points more than doubled at 108.8%. Five forks on 567 stars this early says people are submitting entries, not just reading them.
items.description: A leaderboard for the slowest possible single machine instruction, from the reverse engineer behind the sandsifter processor fuzzer. Instruction analysis normally chases speed; this deliberately searches for the floor. The current x86 champion takes 198 billion cycles, about 62 seconds, by making one instruction load processor state across a deliberately saturated PCIe fabric. Setup can be anything, but only one instruction is scored.

items.name: V4bel/Zapscape
items.brief: Three independent collectors on day one, GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters at once. Stars and forks both up 12.9% in exact lockstep, with Lobsters comments up 25%. Ten forks on 110 stars this early says people are running the exploit to see it work.
items.description: A working exploit and write up for CVE-2026-64561, a guest to host escape in KVM on x86. The bug is a use after free in the shadow MMU, in the recursive path that runs when shadow pages are reclaimed, and a guest can trigger it alone to reach the host kernel with root privilege. It is the third in a series from the same researcher, published after the coordinated embargo ended.

items.brief: Second day and the ratios held. Stars up 8.2%, forks up 12.1%, with forks again outpacing stars: 141 stars and 8 forks yesterday, 172 and 12 today. At that size a dozen people move it, so the direction carries the information rather than the magnitude.
items.description: An open source video editing pipeline from VEED that has no timeline and no interface. Editing happens entirely through a coding agent: cut and reframe footage, layer motion graphics, turn slides or web pages into video. Source footage is optional, since stills and generated media are enough for some briefs. The renderer is free to use but closed, while everything driving it is open.

items.name: googleworkspace/cli
items.brief: GitHub, Homebrew and npm all seeing it at once, and Homebrew is the one that counts. A package manager entry means somebody installed it deliberately rather than starring it in a browser tab. It carries no fixed command list, building itself from Google's Discovery Service at runtime, so it covers whatever the APIs expose today.
items.description: One command line tool covering Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, Docs, Chat and Admin, published in Google's own GitHub organisation but explicitly not an officially supported Google product. It carries no fixed list of commands. It reads Google's Discovery Service at runtime and builds its command surface from whatever the APIs currently expose, so new endpoints appear without a release. Output is structured JSON, and 40 agent skills ship with it.

items.name: garagehq/nightcrawler
items.brief: Forks jumped 32.7% against 23.3% star growth in a day, with watchers up 25%. Three ratios moving together is harder to fake than any one of them spiking. 44 forks on 593 stars is a 7% ratio, so the people finding it are running it rather than filing it.
items.description: An autonomous penetration testing agent that runs entirely on a phone. Left on a network, it discovers hosts, probes services, tests for known vulnerabilities and writes a report, with no cloud connection anywhere in the loop. A 1.2 billion parameter model running on the phone's GPU decides what to do next. It works slowly and one action at a time, which makes it far harder to spot than a scanner that hits every host at once.

Recent pieces analyse 200,000 similes from popular fiction, track a thousand people through their relationships, and map the vocabulary taught to English learners over time. Each essay is a custom built page, which is why the site is cited as a reference for data journalism.

items.brief: Open issues jumped 50% today against 2.8% star growth, so the few people who found it are using it hard enough to break it. A self hosted replacement for a paid crawling service, at 67 stars. Two days since the last push.
items.description: A web scraper written in Rust that returns clean Markdown and metadata from any URL, built as a drop in replacement for Firecrawl and Browserbase. It uses a browser faithful TLS fingerprint to reach pages that block ordinary clients, so a standard page is one fetch and a parse in roughly 300 milliseconds with no headless browser involved. Pages that only render through JavaScript are handled separately.

items.name: wie-project/kakehashi
items.brief: 252 HackerNews points against 64 comments is an unusually low argument ratio, which for infrastructure means people are impressed rather than sceptical. A userspace layer running macOS binaries on Linux ARM64 is the hardest class of project on this list.
items.description: A translation layer that runs macOS ARM64 binaries on Linux, the reverse of the usual direction. It loads Mach-O executables, maps a standalone libSystem and translates BSD system calls at the boundary, with no JIT and no instruction emulator, because both sides are already the same architecture. Real macOS command line tools then run natively on Linux aarch64.

items.name: Claude Opus 5
items.brief: Third on ProductHunt with 450 votes, and the only launch today carrying independent search demand alongside it. That distinction matters more than the rank: a launch is something that happens to a product, while search interest is people going looking of their own accord, and it is the harder of the two to manufacture. Read the search signal, treat the vote count as the noise around it.
items.description: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 model, posted to Product Hunt on release day. The listing is a launch record rather than a product page, so what it measures is how a frontier model release lands with an audience that is mostly building software on top of one.

items.name: worksinprogress.news
items.brief: A magazine covering underrated ideas in science and policy, with 59 HackerNews comments today. Same shape as the other front-page domains on this list: real discussion, a half-percent nudge to its traffic rank, and no evidence yet that separates a good post from a growing publication.
items.description: Works in Progress, a magazine of underrated ideas in science, technology and public policy, published as long essays with the arguments and the data set out in full. Recent pieces cover the pace of medical progress, the upper limits of animal breeding and why unattractive buildings make housing harder to build. Its readership overlaps heavily with the progress studies and policy world.

It is about 8 MB, holds no permissions at all and does not even request internet access, so it cannot send a file anywhere. The gap it fills is that most phones ship several partial viewers that bounce documents to a cloud service to render them.

Each employee gets an isolated workspace with its own memory, files, credentials and permissions, and can also work with the agent in shared channels and projects. The model and the underlying harness are swappable, so a deployment is not tied to one vendor.

items.name: projectpluto.com
items.brief: 79 comments on the front page with a 0.6% Tranco move. Astronomy software with a long history. The pattern across today's domain set is clear and worth naming: HackerNews plus a tiny traffic bump almost always means one popular post, not a rising business.
items.description: Project Pluto supplies astronomical software to amateur and professional astronomers, some commercial and much of it free. Find_Orb takes a set of positional measurements of an asteroid, comet or satellite and determines its orbit; Sat_ID identifies artificial satellites from an observation. These are working tools for people doing orbit determination, and several run in the browser.

items.name: seriot.ch
items.brief: HackerNews points up 20% from a base of 4, with one comment. This is noise that cleared the bar because the domain population was quiet. Listed so the set stays honest about what qualified rather than quietly dropping it.
items.description: The site of Nicolas Seriot, a software engineer who looks for computation in places nobody intended to put any. Recent work shows that three lines of Unicode transliteration rules are Turing complete on the library shipping with every major operating system, and compiles OpenStreetMap into static packs a browser rasterises without a server.

items.name: chriscoyier.net
items.brief: 52 comments, front page, 0.6% traffic gain. Chris Coyier is a well-known web developer; this is his personal site. Fourth example of the same shape today, which is a stronger argument for a gate rule about personal blogs than it is about any of these four domains.
items.description: The personal site of Chris Coyier, who founded CSS-Tricks and co-founded CodePen, and has been one of the most widely read voices in front end web development for fifteen years. The blog runs shorter and more personal than his published work, which is why a post here occasionally reaches a wider audience than the company announcement it refers to.

items.name: maurycyz.com
items.brief: HackerNews comments up 156% to 180 with its front-page rank improving 12%. A personal site pulling that much discussion is usually one essay landing rather than a site becoming popular. Worth reading what it published today; not worth tracking the domain.
items.description: A blog about electronics and software, with occasional chemistry and photography, written by someone who takes apart received wisdom and checks it. A recent piece works through the Phoebus lightbulb cartel story and shows that the usual telling gets the engineering backwards. It also keeps a hand checked list of other blogs verified as not machine generated.

items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Forks up 17.9% and open issues up 25.5% against only 8.5% star growth. The same shape as deltafin: usage outpacing attention. At 1,007 stars with 59 open issues this is a project being deployed rather than starred, and the 46 HackerNews comments suggest the discussion is technical rather than promotional.

items.name: openai/codex-security
items.brief: Still climbing three days after first appearing: stars up 18.8% and forks up 18.3% in twenty four hours, now at 7,237 and 472. Still on the HackerNews front page with 197 comments. Most launches decay by day three and this one has not.
items.description: A command line tool and TypeScript SDK from OpenAI that scans a codebase for security vulnerabilities, validates what it finds and proposes fixes. It runs against OpenAI's models by default but takes any provider, and a deep scan mode can run for hours across many workers. Some categories of finding require approved access before the tool will return them.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Open issues jumped 300% while forks rose 26.8% and stars 15.2%. Issue counts growing faster than stars means people are running it and hitting problems, not admiring the README. That friction is a better adoption signal than a clean tracker, though it also means the project is about to be tested by how fast the maintainer responds.
items.description: A single native binary that runs the complete 2.8 trillion parameter Kimi K3 on consumer hardware with nothing pruned and nothing skipped. Small draft models are allowed to guess ahead for speed, but K3 checks every guess, so quality is never traded away. The published benchmark history shows throughput on an M1 Max laptop rising from 0.014 to 0.29 tokens per second over three weeks.

items.name: mishushakov/desktui
items.brief: Appears in today's corroborated set on both GitHub and HackerNews. Early-stage terminal UI work, and like base-gpui the absolute numbers are small enough that the percentages overstate the case. Listed for completeness rather than conviction.
items.description: A VNC client that draws a remote desktop inside a terminal window as actual pixels, using the Kitty graphics protocol rather than approximating the screen with coloured half blocks. It handles clipboard in both directions in UTF-8, a view only mode, live rescaling and quality settings for slow links. The author built it over a weekend to test what current coding models could do.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Forks grew 41.5% in a day against 18.6% star growth, so people are copying it to build on roughly twice as fast as they are bookmarking it. At 2,196 stars with 326 HackerNews comments it is past the point where a single post explains the numbers.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model on any Apple Silicon Mac in about 2 GB of memory, including the 8 GB machines, instead of loading all 14.3 GB. It keeps the shared core and the cache resident and streams only the experts each token actually needs off the SSD. The runtime, installer, command line tool and Mac app are all written in Swift and Metal, built for this one model rather than wrapping MLX or llama.cpp.

items.name: FrigadeHQ/yap
items.brief: Stars up 8% to 290, forks up 16%, 104 HackerNews points with 43 comments. The numbers are in proportion to each other rather than one of them spiking alone.
items.description: Voice dictation for macOS that runs on the device using Apple's own speech framework, with no account, no API key and no audio leaving the machine. Press a shortcut, talk, press it again, and the text lands in whatever field you were already typing in. Transcripts are kept locally so anything can be copied again later. It is free and open source.

items.name: wassgha/rescript
items.brief: Forks up 11% and open issues up 40% against 16% star growth, with 43 forks on 384 stars. Better than one fork per nine stars, which suggests a tool people modify for their own use rather than adopt as is.
items.description: A video and audio editor where you edit the transcript instead of a timeline. Drop in a file and it is transcribed on the device with per word timestamps and speaker labels; delete a word and the matching piece of media is cut. Nothing is uploaded, and it runs either in a browser or as a desktop application on macOS, Windows and Linux.

items.name: openai/codex-security
items.brief: Forks up 70% and open issues up 84% against 47% star growth, reaching 6,090 stars and 399 forks. Issues climbing faster than stars is the signature of a repository people are running rather than reading, and at this size that means real deployments.

Some categories of finding require approved access before the tool will return them.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Forks up 63% against 42% star growth, on the HackerNews front page with 87 comments. A fork-to-star ratio that high on a 429-star project means people are cloning to modify, not to bookmark. Open issues sitting at 1 says nobody has hit a wall yet, which is either a clean codebase or too early to tell.

items.name: twalichiewicz/HNewhere
items.brief: 419 HackerNews points with comments up 22%, but only 192 stars and 7 forks. Attention running far ahead of adoption: a lot of people found it interesting and very few took it home. It has left the front page, so this is close to its peak unless the star count starts closing the gap.
items.description: A small userscript that shows the Hacker News discussion for whatever page you are reading, if that page has ever been submitted. It closes the gap between finding an article and finding out what people said about it, which normally means a separate search on a separate site.
